notes: A question to a cook rather than a request, which is why it is a concept of its own and not a longer `no-pork` -- the same split the bank already makes between `no-seafood` and `does-it-contain-fish-stock`. `no-pork` names the meat and does not reach the broth: 豚骨 in Japan, 돼지 육수 in Korea, น้ำซุปหมู under nearly every ก๋วยเตี๋ยว and the free soup beside a rice dish in Thailand, 猪骨 stock in southern China. Fill it with the stock word a cook in the country actually uses, and put it in `text`: this template draws no `literal` or `script_alt`, so nothing else reaches the reader.

Shown to a cook or written on an order, so only `text` reaches the reader: this is a shared-width table row and its template draws no `literal` or `script_alt`. Two different failure modes, and the coverage for both has to be inside `text`. In much of east and southeast Asia pork is the default meat and the word for it is not the word for meat, so "no meat" does not cover it. In Europe the word is well known and the dish still arrives with cured pork in it, because ham, bacon and sausage read as seasoning rather than as meat -- so name them: `Sin cerdo ni jamón ni embutidos`, `Sans porc ni lardons`.

Asked of a dish or a shop. The single most useful food question across Indonesia, Malaysia, Turkey, Morocco, Egypt and the Gulf, and askable anywhere -- a traveller who needs it needs it in Japan too. Use the local rendering of "halal" rather than a description where one exists.

The European half of the problem the stock row solves for east Asia, and the same argument: a question to a cook rather than a request, and `no-pork` names the meat. manteca, saindoux, Schmalz, strutto, zsir, banha and น้ำมันหมู go into beans, stews, pastry and stir-fries as *seasoning*, so a cook who hears "no pork" does not count them. Filled per pack rather than as one shared string, because the Spanish translator's warning generalises: `manteca` is lard in Spain and butter in Argentina, so the row has to say `manteca de cerdo`. Shares a cluster with the stock row -- they are the same question about a different vector, so a card with one gains less from the second -- and sits below it, because stock reaches more of the countries this corpus covers.

The one major allergen with no row of its own: `no-peanuts` and `no-nuts` have one each and sesame had to go through `i-am-allergic-to {}`, which is a slot the traveller has to fill in a script they cannot write. Raised by the Hebrew translator -- sesame is one of the allergens Israeli labelling names and tehina is in or beside a very large share of what a visitor is served -- and universal rather than scoped `he`, because sesame is Annex II point 11 of Regulation (EU) 1169/2011 and joined the Codex labelling standard in 2023, so it is declared on a label in most of the countries this corpus covers. Ranked in the appended block rather than at 7 beside the other allergen words, because renumbering seven rows of a file other agents may be editing is the wholesale rewrite `add-a-language.md` forbids. Shown to a cook, so only `text` reaches the reader -- this template draws no `literal` or `script_alt`. Where the oil or the paste is a *different lexeme* the cook would not count, name it inside `text`: Tamil nallennei and Malayalam nallenna, both literally "good oil", are sesame oil and are the default cooking oil, Korean chamgireum is a different word from chamkkae, and tahin, tahina and arde are in the sweets rather than beside them. Where the modifier is transparent -- sesame oil, huile de sesame, sezamove semeno -- the bare word carries it and the row stays short.

The mirror of `is-this-halal`, and universal for the reason that row already gives: kosher is a certification with a visible mark -- a hekhsher badge on the door or the packet -- rather than a judgement a cook makes, so the answer is checkable and the question is worth asking wherever a certified kitchen might be, not only in Israel. Raised by the Hebrew translator. Use the local rendering of "kosher" rather than a description where one exists, and prefer the word the *food* carries over a transliteration of *kashrut*: kashrut is the name of the law, and in a dozen of these languages it is the only form anything has ever printed, which is not a word to show a cook. Sits below halal in `dietary-needs.exclude` and scores below it, because the certification is present in far fewer of the countries this corpus covers -- a card that already carries halal gains less from this than from a first allergen row. Absent from sixteen packs, and the gap is the finding rather than an omission: across the Indic, east African and mainland southeast Asian languages the only attested form is that transliteration of kashrut in an encyclopaedia, so the row is left out rather than calqued.
